responses.strategic_rationale: This 3-year residential parasomnia research unit navigates three fundamental tensions: (1) ecological validity versus operational safety—a domestic setting captures naturalistic behavior but demands continuous overnight staffing and rapid event response; (2) data richness versus annotation burden—tiered sensing (low-burden baseline, enhanced PSG nights, escalation monitoring) maximizes event capture while risking technician and scorer saturation; (3) scientific rigor versus recruitment feasibility—strict inclusion criteria (≥2 episodes/month, specialist confirmation, 70–80% event yield expectation) ensure valid phenotyping but limit participant pool and extend timelines. The levers below address these core trade-offs by controlling scope (facility capacity, participant throughput, sensing granularity), timing (phased enrollment, stay duration caps), and workload distribution (technician staffing, independent scoring, algorithm triage)—the decisions that most directly constrain whether the unit achieves its three aims within budget and timeline.

levers.name: Facility Capacity and Phased Expansion
levers.consequences: Launching with 8 active suites instead of the full 12-suite physical capacity limits initial staffing complexity and allows validation of safety protocols, data quality, and annotation workflows before scaling. Deferring expansion until month 12–18 pilot results are reviewed risks slower enrollment ramp-up and extends the period before achieving target participant throughput of 30–35 per year; premature expansion to 12 suites could strain the 3-person night technician roster and create unmanageable nightly annotation backlogs if event frequency exceeds baseline assumptions.
options: Maintain 8-suite launch indefinitely and scale only if external advisory board confirms post-hoc event-capture rates and technician utilization support 12-suite viability, accepting slower publication timelines and lower total dataset size by month 36.

Commit to 10-suite expansion by month 12 based on pilot metrics (safe staffing ratios, <15% false alarm rate, dual-scorer agreement >85%), hiring one additional technician preemptively in month 6 to phase in coverage.

Activate all 12 suites by month 6 while distributing night coverage across rotating 4-person technician teams and outsourcing annotation of low-priority sensor streams (ambient microphones, environmental logs) to trained undergraduate research assistants, accelerating enrollment but risking quality drift if assistant training is insufficient.
levers.review_lever: Larger capacity enables faster enrollment and richer datasets but multiplies nightly staffing variability and annotation workload, and the three options sidestep how to sustain 12-suite operations if episode capture rates fall below 70% or technician retention falters under shift work.

levers.name: Participant Stay Duration and Event Yield Strategy
levers.consequences: Current protocol allows 2–8 week stays with optional extension to 10 weeks total, targeting 70–80% event capture; this flexibility accommodates natural variation in parasomnia frequency but risks high-cost unproductive admissions if trigger-identification fails. If 20% or more of admissions yield zero adjudicated events, protocol is reviewed and inclusion criteria may tighten, potentially excluding lower-frequency phenotypes and narrowing Aim 2 characterization scope.
options: Standardize to fixed 6-week mandatory stays with no extension option, ensuring uniform data collection windows and predictable participant throughput, but excluding lower-frequency participants and risking incomplete phenotyping of rare cluster patterns.

Implement a mid-stay interim review (week 3–4) with explicit go/no-go criteria: if zero events captured and technician-flagged episodes are absent, discharge the participant and reallocate bed to new admission, capping unproductive stays at 4 weeks and lowering per-participant cost but increasing recruitment pressure and potential bias toward high-frequency sleepers.

Use week-1 and week-2 baseline data to stratify participants into high-likelihood and low-likelihood event-capture groups, then reserve extension slots selectively for low-likelihood participants while admitting high-likelihood participants on shorter fixed 4-week cycles, optimizing bed turnover and study power but requiring predictive models that may not exist early in the pilot.
levers.review_lever: Shorter mandatory stays reduce cost and turnover friction but risk excluding rare episodic phenotypes; longer flexible stays improve event yield but concentrate resources on slow-to-capture participants, and none of the options address whether the 70–80% baseline capture assumption is accurate from month 1.

levers.name: Technician Staffing Model and Annotation Burden
levers.consequences: The current plan specifies 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to cover 8 suites; each technician performs real-time annotation during shifts and participates in post-hoc dual scoring. If event frequency exceeds baseline assumptions or multiple simultaneous events occur, technicians face competing demands (participant safety, live annotation, equipment troubleshooting), potentially degrading inter-rater reliability and increasing burnout. Outsourcing annotation to external scorers reduces technician workload but introduces coordination overhead and potential scoring-quality variability if external raters lack facility-specific training.
options: Hire a dedicated fourth technician (part-time or full-time offset) whose sole role is post-shift annotation and video review, freeing the three night technicians to focus on live monitoring and participant safety, increasing personnel cost by roughly €150–200K over three years but improving scorer agreement and reducing technician turnover.

Train and onboard two independent external sleep medicine technicians as remote dual scorers, compensating them per-event or per-hour to annotate recorded sessions asynchronously, reducing nightly workload conflicts but creating a 48–72 hour lag in event adjudication that delays real-time escalation protocol decisions and introduces single-point-of-failure dependency if external scorers become unavailable.

Cross-train the clinical psychologist and data engineer as secondary scorers for non-complex events (clear arousal-to-movement sequences), reserving full dual-technician scoring for ambiguous events, reducing technician burden but potentially underestimating inter-rater disagreement on subtle sleep-stage transitions and requiring concurrent upskilling time.
levers.review_lever: Dedicated annotation staff prevents safety–annotation conflicts but adds fixed costs; external scorers lower technician burden but introduce lag and quality variability, and the three options do not address how to sustain scoring momentum if event volume or complexity increases beyond current assumptions.

levers.name: Sensing Tier Escalation and Event Detection Automation
levers.consequences: Current protocol uses low-burden nightly monitoring (dry EEG, mattress sensors, infrared cameras, microphones) plus scheduled enhanced PSG on days 1, mid-stay, and final nights, with escalation PSG after technician-flagged events. Heavy reliance on technician visual flagging creates a gatekeeping bottleneck: if technicians miss subtle events or flag false positives, the escalation protocol fails and event yield drops. Deploying automated screening (e.g., movement-anomaly detection from mattress or video, arousal-rate spikes from EEG headbands) reduces technician cognitive load but risks algorithmic false positives that trigger unnecessary PSG escalations, inflating equipment wear and per-night cost.
options: Maintain manual technician flagging as the sole escalation trigger, supplemented by a weekly algorithmic pre-screen (movement-acceleration thresholding on mattress data) that highlights nights for technician re-review but does not automatically trigger PSG, keeping the protocol simple and technician-centric while accepting slower detection of atypical event morphologies.

Deploy a calibrated machine-learning classifier (trained on the initial 100 events captured during the pilot phase) to automatically flag high-confidence movement anomalies during nightly low-burden monitoring, triggering PSG escalation without technician review, reducing latency and detection misses but risking overfitting to the pilot cohort and creating algorithmic bias if event morphology varies across participant subgroups.

Use a two-stage triage system: rapid automated movement detection feeds a technician-in-the-loop dashboard that highlights candidate nights, technician confirms or rejects the candidate in a 5-minute structured review (using a checklist of visual and temporal criteria), and confirmed candidates trigger PSG escalation, balancing automation efficiency with human judgment and enabling post-hoc calibration of the algorithm's sensitivity-specificity trade-off.
levers.review_lever: Technician flagging is labor-intensive and prone to fatigue errors; automated detection accelerates capture but risks false escalations and overfitting, and none of the options guarantee sufficient Aim 3 algorithm training data if pilot events remain rare.

levers.name: Control Group Recruitment and Baseline Benchmarking
levers.consequences: A matched control group of healthy sleepers undergoes identical residential monitoring without the disease inclusion criteria, providing baseline false-positive rates from ambient sensors and movement patterns under normal conditions. This strengthens Aim 3 algorithm validation but requires recruiting and compensating an additional cohort (estimated 15–25 controls), adding approximately €60–100K to the budget and extending recruitment timelines. If controls are not matched adequately (age, sex, BMI, sleep position distribution), their baseline sensor activity may not generalize to the patient population, undermining algorithm specificity benchmarking.
options: Recruit 20–25 healthy controls in a dedicated recruitment phase (months 6–12), matched to the NREM parasomnia cohort on age, sex, and BMI using structured eligibility criteria, monitoring them for 2–3 week residential stays and using their data for algorithm specificity and false-positive calibration, accepting the recruitment complexity but securing robust negative data.

Use historical normative polysomnography data from University Hospital Bonn's sleep clinic database (existing PSG recordings from age-matched controls without sleep disorders) as a proxy baseline for sensor false-positive rates, avoiding new recruitment and cost but sacrificing ecological validity because historical data lacks the identical low-burden sensor stream combination and residential environment exposure.

Enroll controls opportunistically from family members and bed partners of NREM parasomnia participants (with separate informed consent), leveraging existing facility access and reducing recruitment burden, but introducing kinship confounds and potential bias if family members differ systematically in baseline arousal or movement patterns.
levers.review_lever: Controls provide critical specificity benchmarking but are resource-intensive; using historical data is cheaper but less ecologically valid, and recruiting from family introduces confounds that the three options do not adequately isolate.

levers.name: Data Sharing Strategy and Repository Deposition
levers.consequences: The protocol restricts public sharing to de-identified physiological and sensor data (EEG, EMG, mattress sensors, environmental logs) under data use agreements, excluding bedroom video due to privacy constraints. Full repository deposition by month 36 (per the success criteria) requires finalizing de-identification procedures, dataset documentation, and BIDS harmonization by month 30–32, consuming data engineer and PI time for curation. However, strict de-identification may remove clinically relevant context (time-of-night patterns, seasonal trends, medication timings) if overly aggressive, while loose de-identification invites re-identification risk and potential ethics board pushback, delaying public release.
options: Deposit all physiological and sensor data (excluding video) in a recognized open repository (e.g., OpenNeuro, PhysioNet) under BIDS-compatible format with a CC-BY-SA 4.0 license, enabling broad reuse by the sleep neuroscience community but committing to full de-identification, BIDS validation, and metadata curation by month 30, consuming 200+ hours of data engineer time and risking delays if unexpected privacy issues emerge during curation.

Release a tiered dataset: open-access summary statistics and de-identified PSG-only files in a public repository (months 32–36), with full sensor streams (including timing metadata) available under a controlled-access agreement requiring researchers to obtain ethics board approval and sign data use agreements, increasing accessibility controls but creating administrative overhead for the future user support team.

Retain all data within the University of Bonn research data management system under institutional access control, making it available only to collaborators who sign formal data use agreements with the PI, maximizing privacy protection and regulatory certainty but limiting discoverability and reproducibility for the broader community and reducing long-term citation impact.
levers.review_lever: Open deposition maximizes impact but requires aggressive de-identification that risks losing contextual detail; controlled access preserves context but fragments the user community, and the three options do not resolve the trade-off between maximizing privacy and maintaining clinical interpretability.

levers.name: Publication Strategy and Pharma Partnership Timing
levers.consequences: Success criteria include 2–3 peer-reviewed publications by month 36 covering methods and longitudinal characterization; these publications establish scientific credibility and generate preliminary data for the phase-two grant proposal. An optional pharmaceutical industry partnership (offering research funding and potential future drug-development collaboration) carries a 30-day pre-publication comment window for the partner, creating potential publication delays if the partner raises substantial concerns. Early partnership engagement accelerates funding but risks prioritizing pharma interests over publication independence; deferring partnership discussions until month 18–24 preserves editorial autonomy but may delay securing additional resources and reduce timeline flexibility for budget overruns.
options: Secure the pharma partnership by month 3–4, allowing the partner early sight-line into preliminary results and reducing financial risk, but requiring all publication manuscripts to circulate for the 30-day pre-publication comment window, potentially delaying submission timelines and introducing subtle framing pressures aligned with partner commercial interests.

Publish independently through months 1–24 (targeting the methods paper by month 18 and the first longitudinal characterization paper by month 24), then approach pharma partners post-hoc with a demonstrated track record of independent publishing, preserving editorial freedom but accepting the risk that pharmaceutical interest may cool if preliminary results are already public and potentially losing 3–6 months of partnership funding.

Establish a formal data advisory committee with pharma partner representatives, the PI, and external sleep medicine experts, who review manuscripts collaboratively 45 days before submission and provide written comments (rather than a unilateral veto), ensuring partner input without granting veto power, but requiring consensus-building effort and potentially fragmenting publication authority among committee members.
levers.review_lever: Early pharma partnerships fund operations but impose publication veto-adjacent constraints; independent publishing delays partnership activation but preserves autonomy, and none of the options address how to restructure the partnership model if preliminary results diverge from partner expectations or commercial strategy.

responses.strategic_rationale: This parasomnia research unit navigates three core tensions: (1) ecological validity versus experimental control—a domestic environment captures natural behavior but complicates standardized safety protocols; (2) event rarity versus efficiency—infrequent episodes demand long participant stays, but extended occupancy strains facility throughput and budget; (3) clinician liability versus scientific openness—video data and behavioral events raise privacy and safety concerns that conflict with transparent data sharing. The selected levers address these tensions by forcing explicit choices about environmental design trade-offs, participant throughput versus capture quality, technician skill and judgment scope, funding partnerships and publication independence, inter-rater rigor and manual burden, equipment acquisition timing, and control group strategy—each revealing hidden costs and dependencies that generic operational planning masks.

levers.name: Residential Environment Authenticity versus Safety Systematization
levers.consequences: Preserving a genuinely domestic atmosphere (minimal padding, standard furniture, accessible windows) maximizes naturalistic parasomnia behavior and participant comfort, reducing suppression from clinical cues, but introduces continuous safety trade-offs—a participant with uncontrolled wandering requires either restrictive design (padded walls, locked windows) that triggers the clinical-feel suppression, or constant technician presence that limits the number of simultaneously monitored suites. The pilot's false-alarm rate and injury-incident frequency will determine whether the current 8-suite model is sustainable or demands expensive staffing ramp-up.
options: Commit to a minimalist safety envelope—standard residential furniture, unrestricted common areas, full-size windows with silent exit alarms and overnight technician patrols—accepting that severe wandering cases cannot be safely admitted and building exclusion criteria accordingly.

Implement progressive zone restriction—participants sleep in dedicated suites with enhanced safety features (padded edges, monitored egress) but share naturalistic common spaces for meals and day activity, creating a hybrid that isolates risk to designated hours.

Establish a two-tier admission pathway where participants demonstrating controlled wandering in the pre-study night undergo standard monitoring, while those with severe or unpredictable motor behavior are directed to a separate clinical-standard suite with full padding and continuous staff shadowing, accepting the dual-environment operational burden.
levers.review_lever: Minimalist design maximizes ecological validity but transfers safety responsibility entirely to technician vigilance, creating staffing scalability bottlenecks and insurance liability exposure that three options do not resolve—only empirical pilot data will reveal the actual injury rate and technician burnout threshold.

levers.name: Participant Admission Velocity versus Episode Capture Probability
levers.consequences: Shorter target stays (2–3 weeks) allow higher throughput, reaching 50–70 participants faster and generating more diverse phenotypes, but reduce per-participant event yield because parasomnia frequency is variable and some admissions will capture zero events—the protocol currently caps unproductive admissions at 20% before triggering criteria review, forcing a choice between strict preadmission screening (higher cost, slower recruitment) or accepting failed admissions and extending stays reactively (budget overrun). Balancing speed and capture quality determines whether the €3.8M budget achieves the minimum event count for Aim 2 analysis or requires external funding augmentation.
options: Enforce strict preadmission screening using a prospective 4-week home actigraphy run and structured bed-partner interview to confirm ≥3 episodes per week, admitting only high-confidence cases and accepting slower recruitment (20–25 participants per year) with near-certainty of multi-episode capture.

Adopt a variable-stay adaptive model where all participants enter for a standard 4-week baseline, but those reaching zero events by week 3 trigger an automated extension protocol (up to 2 additional weeks, funded from the contingency reserve) with the goal of capturing at least one event per admission.

Implement a rolling cohort with staggered 2-week admissions, accepting 25–30% unproductive stays as inherent noise, and use those cases to build a control-group comparison dataset on what nocturnal behavior looks like in participants who *think* they have parasomnia events but never demonstrate them clinically.
levers.review_lever: Shorter stays reduce cost per participant but amplify the risk of zero-event admissions that generate only baseline sensor data with no episode phenotyping value—none of the three options directly address how to repurpose failed admissions or whether 20% unproductivity is operationally sustainable.

levers.name: Technician Annotation Authority and Real-Time Scoring Rigor
levers.consequences: Empowering night technicians to flag probable parasomnia events in real time (allowing triage escalation and event-driven PSG capture) accelerates clinical responsiveness and preserves sleep-state context, but introduces rater-dependent inconsistency—a tired or undertrained technician may miss subtle confusional arousals or misclassify sleep-stage-specific events, polluting the event-triage training dataset and inflating false-positive rates. The protocol mandates dual independent scoring afterward, but that occurs 48+ hours post-event when polysomnography context is lost and disagreement becomes expensive to adjudicate. Real-time technician judgment is operationally indispensable but methodologically risky without clear competency criteria and quality assurance.
options: Designate technicians as primary event identifiers with explicit training in AASM parasomnia criteria and mandatory weekly inter-rater agreement audits against video review and retrospective PSG analysis, creating a structured quality-feedback loop and accepting that some technicians will never reach ≥80% sensitivity.

Implement a dual-reviewer night model where one technician monitors sensors and participant safety while a second (lower-cost position) reviews video feeds in parallel 30-second-delayed playback, allowing collaborative event flagging and real-time discussion before escalation, increasing labor cost but reducing technician-specific bias.

Restrict technician real-time flagging to behavioral observations only (movement, vocalizations, unusual arousal patterns) without AASM-criteria scoring, reserving all parasomnia classification for the dual independent raters working from synchronized physiological data 24–48 hours post-admission, sacrificing event-driven PSG escalation but eliminating technician classification error.
levers.review_lever: Real-time technician annotation enables clinical response and algorithm training but depends entirely on hire quality and fatigue state—none of the options directly address how to sustain consistent accuracy over 24 months without expensive turnover or whether weekly audits are sufficient to catch systematic bias.

levers.name: Enhanced PSG Montage Deployment Frequency and Sensing Cost Escalation
levers.consequences: Current protocol schedules enhanced PSG (standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, leg EMG) only on three fixed nights per participant (first, mid-stay, final) plus technician-flagged escalation nights; this minimizes per-participant sensor cost and technician calibration overhead, but risks missing the detailed physiological phenotype of events that occur outside scheduled nights, especially if episodes cluster unpredictably. Full continuous PSG would eliminate this blind spot but increases equipment utilization, technician setup time, and per-night cost substantially—the budget constrains the number of available PSG nights within the €3.8M envelope, forcing a choice between broad shallow sampling (all 8 suites nightly with dry EEG only) or deep sampling on fewer nights (full PSG on 3 scheduled nights per participant).
options: Retain the three fixed-night-plus-escalation model but add a fourth scheduled night at day 10 (early mid-stay inflection point where sustained parasomnia frequency patterns emerge), increasing per-participant PSG cost by approximately 25% and accepting that some sporadic events still occur between monitored nights.

Shift to a full-montage PSG-every-night model for the first 2 weeks of each admission, then revert to dry-electrode-only monitoring if no events are captured, backweighting equipment cost to high-yield early weeks and reducing later-stage setup burden while betting that event-free trajectories stabilize by week 3.

Implement a three-tier escalation protocol: baseline dry-EEG nightly, automatic PSG upgrade triggered after the first participant-reported event or technician flag (not contingent on schedule), and full in-situ PSG reactivation within 2 hours if a second event is flagged within 48 hours, making deployment reactive rather than fixed and requiring on-call technician availability.
levers.review_lever: Fixed scheduling guarantees comparability but misses sporadic event phenotypes; fully reactive PSG maximizes capture but requires unsustainable technician availability and equipment turnaround—the three options do not resolve the cost-per-event trade-off or establish how to detect a true event clustering pattern versus random chance.

levers.name: Control Group Recruitment Scope and Baseline Contamination Risk
levers.consequences: The current plan includes matched controls under identical residential monitoring to benchmark event-triage tool false-positive rates against normal nocturnal behavior; this is methodologically essential for tool validation but requires recruiting and housing healthy adults (not parasomnia patients) for 2–8 week residential stays, a recruiting and safety challenge orthogonal to the patient pathway. Expanding the control cohort to 20–30 participants provides robust statistical power for false-positive thresholding but doubles staff coordination and facility occupancy complexity; conversely, minimal controls (n=5–10) compress costs but leave the false-positive rate estimate statistically underpowered, potentially biasing downstream algorithm specificity claims.
options: Recruit a small fixed control cohort (n=8–10) from sleep clinic volunteers, conduct their monitoring synchronously with patient admissions to share technician time, and accept statistical power limitations, focusing false-positive analysis on the aggregate absence of events rather than on individual-level noise characterization.

Establish a dedicated rolling control-recruitment pathway parallel to patient enrollment, aiming for 1 control participant per 3 patient participants over the 3-year window (approximately 20–25 controls), with separate scheduling to avoid overnight cross-contamination and allowing extended sensor-baseline analysis across seasons and circadian phases.

Use existing University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic healthy volunteers (staff, students, and registered research volunteers) rather than new external recruitment, compensating them at a lower per-night rate (€40 versus €80) and conducting all control monitoring in a single dedicated suite with fixed scheduling (e.g., weekly cohorts), trading recruitment flexibility for operational simplicity and data homogeneity.
levers.review_lever: Robust controls are methodologically necessary but competing for facility resources and technician time with the primary parasomnia cohort—none of the options clarify how control-group monitoring interleaves with patient care or whether a 1:3 ratio is actually achievable without facility expansion.

levers.name: Dual-Rater Independence and Manual Scoring Throughput Sustainability
levers.consequences: The protocol mandates two independent AASM-trained raters score all nights and all flagged events post-hoc, ensuring rigorous event adjudication and enabling inter-rater reliability reporting; this is essential for credibility but creates a labor bottleneck—if a single trained rater can score approximately 4–5 participant-nights per week (assuming 8 hours per night of polysomnography data), then 50–70 participants with 2–8 weeks each generate a scoring backlog of 500+ nights, requiring ~2.5 FTE rater-years over three years. The €3.8M budget allocates personnel funds for the team but independent dual scoring is often outsourced or requires hiring additional scorers, compressing available funds for other functions or extending publication timelines.
options: Embed independent scoring as a postdoctoral researcher responsibility, assigning both sleep-neurophysiology and computational-neuroscience postdocs to split the 500+ night-scoring workload with the PI spot-checking 10% for quality, accepting that rater-pair turnaround extends 6–12 months post-data-collection and publication lag expands accordingly.

Establish a partnership with a certified sleep-scoring service (e.g., through a collaborating sleep center or commercial lab), outsourcing 70–80% of dual-rater workload at a per-night cost of €40–60 per night, preserving internal postdoc time for algorithm development and reducing the publication timeline but incurring a variable cost line-item that must come from existing budget allocations.

Implement a three-person scoring hierarchy where one lead rater (the PI) independently scores all nights flagged as events, a second trained rater independently scores a stratified 60% random sample, and agreement/disagreement patterns trigger selective third-rater adjudication only for discordant cases (estimated at 10–15% of all nights), reducing total scoring FTE to ~1.5 rater-years but introducing composite rater definitions and potential bias toward lead-rater decisions.
levers.review_lever: Dual independent scoring is a methodological non-negotiable but creates labor and cost contingencies that the three options manage differently—none directly address how to prevent rater fatigue or drift over 36 months or establish inter-rater reliability targets.

levers.name: Publication Timing and Pharma Partnership Conditionality
levers.consequences: The plan positions pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside: if secured, the pharma partner receives a 30-day pre-publication comment window and retains no veto rights, but the relationship creates perception of bias and may trigger ethical review scrutiny or media criticism regarding parasomnia treatment commercialization. Alternatively, declining pharma funding preserves full academic independence but eliminates potential €300K–500K funding augmentation and reduces the probability of rapid translation to drug-development pathways; timing of early publications (methods paper at month 18, phenotyping data at month 24) may be delayed or accelerated depending on whether pharma escalation happens, introducing a strategic coordination point that affects both scientific credibility and financial runway.
options: Commit to pharma partnership before month 6, negotiate the comment-window terms and conflict-of-interest disclosures upfront, and coordinate publication schedules to satisfy both academic (journal timelines) and industry (regulatory planning) calendars, accepting the reputational trade-off but guaranteeing extended funding and ensuring first publications occur within the grant timeline.

Delay pharma partnership negotiation until month 18 (after the methods-validation publication), preserving full independent ownership of early work and allowing the academic team to establish the facility's reputation and event-capture capability before industry engagement, accepting financial constraint through year two but maintaining editorial control and optionality.

Maintain an explicit no-pharma-partnership policy throughout the 3-year window, emphasizing scientific independence in all publications and external communications, fully absorbing the €3.8M project from DFG and University of Bonn funding and accepting tighter budget margins (larger contingency depletion) if enrollment or event-capture targets slip.
levers.review_lever: Pharma partnership accelerates funding but introduces publication-timing constraints and conflict-of-interest complexity; full independence preserves credibility but narrows financial flexibility—the three options do not address whether early publication of preliminary data inhibits or enables subsequent partnership.

responses.strategic_rationale: This parasomnia research unit must balance three foundational tensions: capturing rare, naturalistic events in a home-like setting while maintaining clinical safety and operational rigor; scaling participant throughput without compromising data quality or technician annotation capacity; and publishing credible longitudinal phenotyping work within a 3-year window despite inherent delays in event capture, multi-rater scoring, and algorithm validation. The critical levers below address recruitment-to-retention funnel integrity, the trade-off between sensing resolution and false-alarm burden on night staff, the sustainability of manual annotation workflows as event volume grows, the timing of methodological publication relative to later intervention-study funding, the balance between domestic authenticity and systematic data completeness, the strategic sequencing of control-group enrollment, and the governance of pharmacology-industry partnerships without compromising academic independence.

levers.name: Sleep History Depth Versus Pre-Admission Screening Speed
levers.consequences: Detailed pre-admission clinical interviews (multi-hour, including structured collateral interviews with bed partners and prior sleep record review) will identify high-confidence NREM parasomnia cases more reliably, reducing the risk of misclassified admissions that consume weeks without yielding genuine events. However, this depth extends the recruitment-to-admission timeline by 4–8 weeks per participant, compressing the usable observation window within the 2–8 week (capped at 10 weeks total) stay and potentially forcing earlier discharge decisions with fewer captured events.
options: Conduct comprehensive pre-admission interviews with mandatory bed-partner corroboration and review of any prior polysomnography or sleep diaries, accepting a 6–8 week screen-to-admission lag to maximize diagnostic confidence.

Use a streamlined phone-based screening interview with documented self-reported episode frequency and exclusion-checklist adjudication, admitting candidates within 2–3 weeks at the cost of occasional misclassified admissions.

Implement a two-tier model: rapid phone screening to gate admission within 3 weeks, then a full clinical interview during the first stay-day to confirm diagnosis in real time, re-enrolling misclassified cases as de facto low-event participants.
levers.review_lever: Thorough pre-screening maximizes diagnostic confidence but sacrifices recruitment velocity and usable stay-days for genuine events; streamlined intake risks wasting bed capacity on non-parasomnia cases, and the two-tier hybrid trades first-night data quality for enrollment speed without resolving the misclassification trade-off itself.

levers.name: Extended Stay Duration for Low-Event Participants versus Facility Throughput
levers.consequences: Extending stays up to 10 weeks total (after initial period with zero events) preserves the opportunity to capture at least one event from otherwise low-frequency participants and supports the 70–80% yield target mentioned in planning. However, each extended stay occupies one of eight suites for an additional 2 weeks, reducing absolute participant throughput and delaying the recruitment of fresh participants, which in turn delays event capture diversity and compresses the 3-year timeline for achieving 50–70 admissions.
options: Offer all zero-event participants the full 2-week extension option (up to 10 weeks total) with continued €80 nightly compensation, treating extended stays as a fair and thorough recruitment strategy despite reduced throughput.

Limit extensions to participants showing borderline event evidence (partial captures, questionnaire-reported episodes not yet confirmed) or strong clinical indication, using strict criteria to reserve facility capacity for fresh admissions.

Discontinue participants after the initial 2–8 week period regardless of event capture, then re-enroll low-event cases in a dedicated second-admission cohort if budget permits, separating throughput scheduling from per-participant stay length.
levers.review_lever: Extending stays for low-event participants increases event yield per person but reduces fresh-participant throughput and delays recruitment-phase completion; selective extension requires predictive criteria that may not exist early in the program, and dedicated second-admission cohorts add operational complexity without clear return.

levers.name: Night Technician Real-Time Annotation Depth versus Event-Triage Algorithm Maturity
levers.consequences: Technicians performing detailed, AASM-criteria-aligned annotation during nights (in real time) ensure gold-standard scoring and can flag borderline events for enhanced PSG escalation nights immediately. This rigor, however, increases per-shift cognitive load during live monitoring and diverts attention from suite safety checks and equipment troubleshooting; as event volume grows from 50–70 participants, cumulative annotation backlog and dual-rater review demands will exceed staffing capacity unless the semi-automated event-triage tool matures sufficiently to pre-filter false positives and rank probable events.
options: Require technicians to perform full AASM-criteria scoring during night shifts for all flagged events, prioritizing annotation accuracy and enabling immediate escalation decisions, accepting that by year three annotation throughput may create a 2–4 week scoring lag as event volume accumulates.

Deploy a lightweight event-triage prototype early (month 4–6) to rank flagged events by parasomnia probability, instructing technicians to perform detailed AASM annotation only on high-ranked candidates during the shift, deferring borderline events to post-hoc dual-rater review and accepting lower immediate escalation confidence.

Separate night technician duties entirely: designate two shifts as "monitoring and flagging only" (no shift-time annotation), with all detailed scoring delegated to a dedicated daytime annotation team reviewing time-stamped event flags within 24 hours, reducing night-shift cognitive load but requiring a fourth technician or outsourced scoring contractor.
levers.review_lever: Full real-time annotation sustains scoring rigor but creates unsustainable backlog as event volume grows; early algorithm deployment reduces night-shift burden but risks missing clinically important events during the triage-tool validation phase, and separate day-shift annotation staff adds headcount or external costs without addressing the upstream problem of distinguishing true parasomnia events from sensor noise.

levers.name: Matched Control Group Enrollment Timing and Baseline Contamination Risk
levers.consequences: Recruiting and admitting a matched control cohort in parallel with case recruitment (from month 3 onward) provides immediate baseline comparisons for sensor false-positive rates and normal nocturnal arousal patterns, strengthening the benchmark claims for the event-triage tool. However, control-group participants follow identical dormitory routines and share common environmental exposures (e.g., fire alarm tests, construction noise, ambient light cycles) with case participants, creating correlated baseline data that may not be truly independent and introducing the risk that control groups inadvertently develop documented sleep disturbances through facility-induced stress or social effect, contaminating the "normal" baseline.
options: Enroll control participants on a matched schedule from month 3, aiming for 15–20 controls by month 24 (equivalent to ~30% of expected case enrollment), accepting shared environmental exposures and using statistical covariance adjustment to account for facility-level confounds.

Delay control enrollment until month 12 after case-participant monitoring patterns and facility-level environmental variability are well-characterized, allowing prospective matching on documented facility conditions and reducing baseline-contamination risk at the cost of fewer baseline observations in the early algorithm-development phase.

Recruit control participants from a non-residential outpatient setting (one night at a nearby hospital sleep lab with identical sensor montage and synchronized EEG-BIDS format) rather than residential admission, eliminating facility-induced stress contamination but forgoing the authentic nocturnal-behavior parallels of same-facility control data.
levers.review_lever: Parallel residential control enrollment accelerates baseline characterization but introduces facility-level contamination and environmental correlation; delayed enrollment reduces baseline noise but compresses algorithm-validation data, and outpatient controls eliminate contamination at the cost of losing the ecological equivalence of shared-facility monitoring conditions.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Engagement Scope and Publication Autonomy Preservation
levers.consequences: Early engagement of a pharma industry partner (e.g., for medication-response phenotyping or future intervention studies) unlocks co-funding, regulatory expertise, and potential phase-two expansion capital, accelerating financial sustainability beyond the 3-year DFG grant. However, a partner with direct commercial interest in parasomnia-treatment outcomes may press for accelerated publication timelines, influence which findings are highlighted, or restrict secondary analyses and data-access terms, compromising the academic program's ability to publish methodological critiques or null results that might discourage use of the partner's in-development compounds.
options: Pursue a full pharmaceutical partnership from month 6, with the partner contributing €500K–€1M in co-funding and having operational input (e.g., recruitment criteria, endpoints) on a defined subset of participants (e.g., 15–20 intervention-ready cases), while maintaining arm's-length publication rights per the stated 30-day pre-publication comment window only.

Defer pharma engagement until month 18 after methodological validation is complete and Aims 1–2 publications are submitted, limiting partner involvement to future phase-two expansion and preserving full academic publication autonomy for the pilot phase.

Establish a lightweight pharma liaison role (quarterly meetings, data-sharing MOU under standard academic templates) with no direct funding or operational input, preserving complete editorial independence at the cost of foregoing co-funding and stronger pharma partnership leverage for later expansion.
levers.review_lever: Early pharma engagement accelerates funding but risks publication-autonomy conflicts and outcome-driven biases; delayed engagement preserves methodological independence but leaves the €800K year-three contingency shortfall unresolved, and lightweight liaison avoids conflicts but fails to secure additional capital for operational or enrollment expansion.

levers.name: Sensor-Tier Deployment Sequencing and Detection-Specificity Trade-Offs
levers.consequences: Rolling out enhanced PSG (scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, leg EMG) on only three nights per participant (first, mid-stay, final) provides high-resolution physiological context for a subset of total participant-nights, reducing equipment wear, technician setup burden, and data storage costs. However, this sparse sampling misses the temporal density of episodes that occur on non-PSG nights, limiting the ability to characterize within-participant clustering or circadian patterns; conversely, deploying full PSG nightly for all participants would saturate the resource budget (~€450K equipment + storage/analysis overhead) and overwhelm annotation capacity unless automation tools mature significantly.
options: Implement the planned three-night PSG schedule (first, mid-stay, final) uniformly for all participants, reserving escalation-night full PSG exclusively for technician-flagged events and accepting that non-PSG nights rely on lower-resolution sensing and may miss subtle polysomnographic features.

Deploy full PSG nightly for a smaller "intensive phenotyping" sub-cohort (e.g., first 12–15 high-yield participants) and light-sensing-only for remaining participants, building a rich dataset for algorithm training while preserving resource allocation for larger throughput.

Use a dynamic PSG-scheduling rule: schedule three fixed nights per participant initially, but escalate to nightly PSG after a confirmed event is captured on any scheduled or escalation night, concentrating high-resolution monitoring on proven high-event-frequency participants.
levers.review_lever: Three-night scheduled PSG balances resource constraints but sacrifices temporal event density and within-participant clustering insights; intensive sub-cohorts create a heterogeneous data structure that complicates pooled analysis and algorithm generalization, and dynamic escalation-based PSG concentrates resources on already-productive participants, potentially undercapturing rare-event morphology in low-frequency cases.

levers.name: Protocol Ceiling Trigger and Recruitment-Criteria Recalibration Pathway
levers.consequences: The protocol mandates a recruitment-criteria review if unproductive admissions (zero captured events) exceed 20%, theoretically safeguarding against systematic misclassification. However, triggering a review at month 12–15 (after ~25 admissions, assuming 20% unproductive = 5 misclassified cases) consumes precious time, requires PI and advisory board consensus on revised inclusion criteria, and may force a partial restart of the vetting process, compressing the remaining operational months and jeopardizing the 50–70 enrollment target. Conversely, accepting a higher unproductive ceiling (e.g., 25–30%) reduces review friction but squanders stay-bed capacity on non-events, directly eroding the effective event-capture dataset.
options: Enforce the 20% unproductive ceiling strictly, triggering an immediate protocol amendment and criteria-revision cycle when 5 misclassified admissions are documented, with PI and advisory board review completed within 4 weeks to minimize operational disruption and enable rapid re-recruitment.

Relax the ceiling to 25% unproductive admissions, reducing the likelihood of a formal review trigger and preserving enrollment momentum, while conducting a quarterly informal assessment of misclassification patterns (e.g., differential rates by referral source) to inform iterative tightening of screening interview questions.

Use a rolling predictive model: by month 9, analyze early admission data for demographic or clinical predictors of zero-event outcomes, then implement a triage algorithm in the screening process to preferentially enroll high-predicted-yield candidates, avoiding a protocol-level review while proactively filtering for event-yield likelihood.
levers.review_lever: Strict 20% ceiling enforcement triggers timely course-correction but disrupts recruitment momentum mid-program; relaxed ceilings preserve operational flow but tolerate continued misclassification waste, and predictive triage shifts the burden from post-hoc review to screening sophistication without addressing the fundamental uncertainty of event frequency in low-event phenotypes.

levers.name: Multi-Site Expansion Feasibility and Replication Rigor Trade-Offs
levers.consequences: Launching a second residential parasomnia unit (e.g., at another German university hospital or international partner institution) by year two would accelerate participant throughput, diversify recruitment channels, and strengthen generalizability of findings across sites and clinical populations. However, each new site requires independent ethics approval, facility renovation or lease, staff hiring and training, technician cross-site calibration for annotation consistency, and a dual-site data governance and QA structure; the replication burden may deflate the central Bonn facility's operational momentum and introduce site-level heterogeneity in equipment, protocols, and data quality that complicates pooled phenotyping analysis unless rigorous standardization is enforced.
options: Maintain the single Bonn facility through year three, concentrating all effort on operational excellence, high-quality data, and reliable annotation consistency, then propose a multi-site expansion phase-two grant leveraging Bonn methodology as the gold-standard template.

Establish a second site by month 15 (year two) in partnership with a nearby sleep center, replicating the Bonn protocol and sensor montage while maintaining tight data-sharing governance and coordinated technician training to ensure cross-site annotation reliability from inception.

Develop a lightweight "satellite site" model: partner with 1–2 sleep clinics to perform residential stays using Bonn's EEG-BIDS format and lower-tier sensing (dry-electrode EEG + video only, omitting mattress sensors or ambient microphones), with all annotation and event triage conducted remotely by Bonn-based scorers, reducing site-level overhead at the cost of reduced physiological resolution at satellite locations.
levers.review_lever: Single-site focus ensures methodological rigor and annotation consistency but caps throughput at ~60–70 participants and forfeits early multi-site generalizability; parallel second-site expansion accelerates enrollment but introduces coordination complexity and cross-site QA burdens, and lightweight satellite sites reduce on-site overhead but create a two-tier data-quality structure that may confound later pooled analysis.

levers.name: Preliminary Findings Dissemination Timing and Grant-Renewal Positioning
levers.consequences: Publishing interim Aim 1 methods-validation results (facility safety, operational sustainability) by month 18–20 demonstrates proof-of-concept to funders and journals, strengthening a phase-two renewal proposal and establishing the Bonn facility as a credible infrastructure asset. However, premature publication of incomplete phenotyping data (Aim 2 longitudinal characterization) or early algorithm benchmarks (Aim 3 event-triage performance) may invite methodological criticism if the findings are based on <30 participants or <50 adjudicated events, or may be scooped by competing groups if competitors are tracking the same outcome space.
options: Publish an Aim 1 methods-paper at month 18–20 documenting facility validation, technician protocols, and sensor-synchronization methodology, holding Aim 2 and Aim 3 publications until month 30+ when the full cohort and event dataset are mature, staggering outputs to maintain narrative momentum without premature claims.

Defer all publications until month 28–30 to present integrated Aim 1–2–3 findings in a unified high-impact submission, maximizing per-publication credibility and impact factor at the cost of risking a 12–18 month publication gap that may disadvantage grant-renewal perception of scientific momentum.

Release quarterly technical bulletins or preprints (non-peer-reviewed) documenting emerging Aim 1–2 findings, participant enrollment milestones, and algorithm development progress from month 15 onward, building visible momentum for grant reviewers while preserving the option for formal peer-review publications later and managing reader expectations around preliminary maturity.
levers.review_lever: Early Aim 1 publication (month 18) establishes credibility for renewal proposals but risks exposing incomplete Aim 2–3 data to premature critique; full-integration publishing preserves narrative rigor but creates a long publication silence that may undermine grant-renewal perception, and quarterly preprints increase visibility but blur the signal of peer-reviewed output and may provoke questions about data-embargo policies.

levers.name: Facility Capacity and Phased Expansion
levers.consequences: Launching with 8 active suites instead of the full 12-suite physical capacity limits initial staffing complexity and allows validation of safety protocols, data quality, and annotation workflows before scaling. Deferring expansion until month 12–18 pilot results are reviewed risks slower enrollment ramp-up and extends the period before achieving target participant throughput of 30–35 per year; premature expansion to 12 suites could strain the 3-person night technician roster and create unmanageable nightly annotation backlogs if event frequency exceeds baseline assumptions.
options: Maintain 8-suite launch indefinitely and scale only if external advisory board confirms post-hoc event-capture rates and technician utilization support 12-suite viability, accepting slower publication timelines and lower total dataset size by month 36.

Commit to 10-suite expansion by month 12 based on pilot metrics (safe staffing ratios, <15% false alarm rate, dual-scorer agreement >85%), hiring one additional technician preemptively in month 6 to phase in coverage.

Activate all 12 suites by month 6 while distributing night coverage across rotating 4-person technician teams and outsourcing annotation of low-priority sensor streams (ambient microphones, environmental logs) to trained undergraduate research assistants, accelerating enrollment but risking quality drift if assistant training is insufficient.
levers.review: Larger capacity enables faster enrollment and richer datasets but multiplies nightly staffing variability and annotation workload, and the three options sidestep how to sustain 12-suite operations if episode capture rates fall below 70% or technician retention falters under shift work.

levers.name: Participant Stay Duration and Event Yield Strategy
levers.consequences: Current protocol allows 2–8 week stays with optional extension to 10 weeks total, targeting 70–80% event capture; this flexibility accommodates natural variation in parasomnia frequency but risks high-cost unproductive admissions if trigger-identification fails. If 20% or more of admissions yield zero adjudicated events, protocol is reviewed and inclusion criteria may tighten, potentially excluding lower-frequency phenotypes and narrowing Aim 2 characterization scope.
options: Standardize to fixed 6-week mandatory stays with no extension option, ensuring uniform data collection windows and predictable participant throughput, but excluding lower-frequency participants and risking incomplete phenotyping of rare cluster patterns.

Implement a mid-stay interim review (week 3–4) with explicit go/no-go criteria: if zero events captured and technician-flagged episodes are absent, discharge the participant and reallocate bed to new admission, capping unproductive stays at 4 weeks and lowering per-participant cost but increasing recruitment pressure and potential bias toward high-frequency sleepers.

Use week-1 and week-2 baseline data to stratify participants into high-likelihood and low-likelihood event-capture groups, then reserve extension slots selectively for low-likelihood participants while admitting high-likelihood participants on shorter fixed 4-week cycles, optimizing bed turnover and study power but requiring predictive models that may not exist early in the pilot.
levers.review: Shorter mandatory stays reduce cost and turnover friction but risk excluding rare episodic phenotypes; longer flexible stays improve event yield but concentrate resources on slow-to-capture participants, and none of the options address whether the 70–80% baseline capture assumption is accurate from month 1.

levers.name: Technician Staffing Model and Annotation Burden
levers.consequences: The current plan specifies 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to cover 8 suites; each technician performs real-time annotation during shifts and participates in post-hoc dual scoring. If event frequency exceeds baseline assumptions or multiple simultaneous events occur, technicians face competing demands (participant safety, live annotation, equipment troubleshooting), potentially degrading inter-rater reliability and increasing burnout. Outsourcing annotation to external scorers reduces technician workload but introduces coordination overhead and potential scoring-quality variability if external raters lack facility-specific training.
options: Hire a dedicated fourth technician (part-time or full-time offset) whose sole role is post-shift annotation and video review, freeing the three night technicians to focus on live monitoring and participant safety, increasing personnel cost by roughly €150–200K over three years but improving scorer agreement and reducing technician turnover.

Train and onboard two independent external sleep medicine technicians as remote dual scorers, compensating them per-event or per-hour to annotate recorded sessions asynchronously, reducing nightly workload conflicts but creating a 48–72 hour lag in event adjudication that delays real-time escalation protocol decisions and introduces single-point-of-failure dependency if external scorers become unavailable.

Cross-train the clinical psychologist and data engineer as secondary scorers for non-complex events (clear arousal-to-movement sequences), reserving full dual-technician scoring for ambiguous events, reducing technician burden but potentially underestimating inter-rater disagreement on subtle sleep-stage transitions and requiring concurrent upskilling time.
levers.review: Dedicated annotation staff prevents safety–annotation conflicts but adds fixed costs; external scorers lower technician burden but introduce lag and quality variability, and the three options do not address how to sustain scoring momentum if event volume or complexity increases beyond current assumptions.

levers.name: Sensing Tier Escalation and Event Detection Automation
levers.consequences: Current protocol uses low-burden nightly monitoring (dry EEG, mattress sensors, infrared cameras, microphones) plus scheduled enhanced PSG on days 1, mid-stay, and final nights, with escalation PSG after technician-flagged events. Heavy reliance on technician visual flagging creates a gatekeeping bottleneck: if technicians miss subtle events or flag false positives, the escalation protocol fails and event yield drops. Deploying automated screening (e.g., movement-anomaly detection from mattress or video, arousal-rate spikes from EEG headbands) reduces technician cognitive load but risks algorithmic false positives that trigger unnecessary PSG escalations, inflating equipment wear and per-night cost.
options: Maintain manual technician flagging as the sole escalation trigger, supplemented by a weekly algorithmic pre-screen (movement-acceleration thresholding on mattress data) that highlights nights for technician re-review but does not automatically trigger PSG, keeping the protocol simple and technician-centric while accepting slower detection of atypical event morphologies.

Deploy a calibrated machine-learning classifier (trained on the initial 100 events captured during the pilot phase) to automatically flag high-confidence movement anomalies during nightly low-burden monitoring, triggering PSG escalation without technician review, reducing latency and detection misses but risking overfitting to the pilot cohort and creating algorithmic bias if event morphology varies across participant subgroups.

Use a two-stage triage system: rapid automated movement detection feeds a technician-in-the-loop dashboard that highlights candidate nights, technician confirms or rejects the candidate in a 5-minute structured review (using a checklist of visual and temporal criteria), and confirmed candidates trigger PSG escalation, balancing automation efficiency with human judgment and enabling post-hoc calibration of the algorithm's sensitivity-specificity trade-off.
levers.review: Technician flagging is labor-intensive and prone to fatigue errors; automated detection accelerates capture but risks false escalations and overfitting, and none of the options guarantee sufficient Aim 3 algorithm training data if pilot events remain rare.

levers.name: Control Group Recruitment and Baseline Benchmarking
levers.consequences: A matched control group of healthy sleepers undergoes identical residential monitoring without the disease inclusion criteria, providing baseline false-positive rates from ambient sensors and movement patterns under normal conditions. This strengthens Aim 3 algorithm validation but requires recruiting and compensating an additional cohort (estimated 15–25 controls), adding approximately €60–100K to the budget and extending recruitment timelines. If controls are not matched adequately (age, sex, BMI, sleep position distribution), their baseline sensor activity may not generalize to the patient population, undermining algorithm specificity benchmarking.
options: Recruit 20–25 healthy controls in a dedicated recruitment phase (months 6–12), matched to the NREM parasomnia cohort on age, sex, and BMI using structured eligibility criteria, monitoring them for 2–3 week residential stays and using their data for algorithm specificity and false-positive calibration, accepting the recruitment complexity but securing robust negative data.

Use historical normative polysomnography data from University Hospital Bonn's sleep clinic database (existing PSG recordings from age-matched controls without sleep disorders) as a proxy baseline for sensor false-positive rates, avoiding new recruitment and cost but sacrificing ecological validity because historical data lacks the identical low-burden sensor stream combination and residential environment exposure.

Enroll controls opportunistically from family members and bed partners of NREM parasomnia participants (with separate informed consent), leveraging existing facility access and reducing recruitment burden, but introducing kinship confounds and potential bias if family members differ systematically in baseline arousal or movement patterns.
levers.review: Controls provide critical specificity benchmarking but are resource-intensive; using historical data is cheaper but less ecologically valid, and recruiting from family introduces confounds that the three options do not adequately isolate.

levers.name: Data Sharing Strategy and Repository Deposition
levers.consequences: The protocol restricts public sharing to de-identified physiological and sensor data (EEG, EMG, mattress sensors, environmental logs) under data use agreements, excluding bedroom video due to privacy constraints. Full repository deposition by month 36 (per the success criteria) requires finalizing de-identification procedures, dataset documentation, and BIDS harmonization by month 30–32, consuming data engineer and PI time for curation. However, strict de-identification may remove clinically relevant context (time-of-night patterns, seasonal trends, medication timings) if overly aggressive, while loose de-identification invites re-identification risk and potential ethics board pushback, delaying public release.
options: Deposit all physiological and sensor data (excluding video) in a recognized open repository (e.g., OpenNeuro, PhysioNet) under BIDS-compatible format with a CC-BY-SA 4.0 license, enabling broad reuse by the sleep neuroscience community but committing to full de-identification, BIDS validation, and metadata curation by month 30, consuming 200+ hours of data engineer time and risking delays if unexpected privacy issues emerge during curation.

Release a tiered dataset: open-access summary statistics and de-identified PSG-only files in a public repository (months 32–36), with full sensor streams (including timing metadata) available under a controlled-access agreement requiring researchers to obtain ethics board approval and sign data use agreements, increasing accessibility controls but creating administrative overhead for the future user support team.

Retain all data within the University of Bonn research data management system under institutional access control, making it available only to collaborators who sign formal data use agreements with the PI, maximizing privacy protection and regulatory certainty but limiting discoverability and reproducibility for the broader community and reducing long-term citation impact.
levers.review: Open deposition maximizes impact but requires aggressive de-identification that risks losing contextual detail; controlled access preserves context but fragments the user community, and the three options do not resolve the trade-off between maximizing privacy and maintaining clinical interpretability.

levers.name: Publication Strategy and Pharma Partnership Timing
levers.consequences: Success criteria include 2–3 peer-reviewed publications by month 36 covering methods and longitudinal characterization; these publications establish scientific credibility and generate preliminary data for the phase-two grant proposal. An optional pharmaceutical industry partnership (offering research funding and potential future drug-development collaboration) carries a 30-day pre-publication comment window for the partner, creating potential publication delays if the partner raises substantial concerns. Early partnership engagement accelerates funding but risks prioritizing pharma interests over publication independence; deferring partnership discussions until month 18–24 preserves editorial autonomy but may delay securing additional resources and reduce timeline flexibility for budget overruns.
options: Secure the pharma partnership by month 3–4, allowing the partner early sight-line into preliminary results and reducing financial risk, but requiring all publication manuscripts to circulate for the 30-day pre-publication comment window, potentially delaying submission timelines and introducing subtle framing pressures aligned with partner commercial interests.

Publish independently through months 1–24 (targeting the methods paper by month 18 and the first longitudinal characterization paper by month 24), then approach pharma partners post-hoc with a demonstrated track record of independent publishing, preserving editorial freedom but accepting the risk that pharmaceutical interest may cool if preliminary results are already public and potentially losing 3–6 months of partnership funding.

Establish a formal data advisory committee with pharma partner representatives, the PI, and external sleep medicine experts, who review manuscripts collaboratively 45 days before submission and provide written comments (rather than a unilateral veto), ensuring partner input without granting veto power, but requiring consensus-building effort and potentially fragmenting publication authority among committee members.
levers.review: Early pharma partnerships fund operations but impose publication veto-adjacent constraints; independent publishing delays partnership activation but preserves autonomy, and none of the options address how to restructure the partnership model if preliminary results diverge from partner expectations or commercial strategy.

levers.name: Residential Environment Authenticity versus Safety Systematization
levers.consequences: Preserving a genuinely domestic atmosphere (minimal padding, standard furniture, accessible windows) maximizes naturalistic parasomnia behavior and participant comfort, reducing suppression from clinical cues, but introduces continuous safety trade-offs—a participant with uncontrolled wandering requires either restrictive design (padded walls, locked windows) that triggers the clinical-feel suppression, or constant technician presence that limits the number of simultaneously monitored suites. The pilot's false-alarm rate and injury-incident frequency will determine whether the current 8-suite model is sustainable or demands expensive staffing ramp-up.
options: Commit to a minimalist safety envelope—standard residential furniture, unrestricted common areas, full-size windows with silent exit alarms and overnight technician patrols—accepting that severe wandering cases cannot be safely admitted and building exclusion criteria accordingly.

Implement progressive zone restriction—participants sleep in dedicated suites with enhanced safety features (padded edges, monitored egress) but share naturalistic common spaces for meals and day activity, creating a hybrid that isolates risk to designated hours.

Establish a two-tier admission pathway where participants demonstrating controlled wandering in the pre-study night undergo standard monitoring, while those with severe or unpredictable motor behavior are directed to a separate clinical-standard suite with full padding and continuous staff shadowing, accepting the dual-environment operational burden.
levers.review: Minimalist design maximizes ecological validity but transfers safety responsibility entirely to technician vigilance, creating staffing scalability bottlenecks and insurance liability exposure that three options do not resolve—only empirical pilot data will reveal the actual injury rate and technician burnout threshold.

levers.name: Participant Admission Velocity versus Episode Capture Probability
levers.consequences: Shorter target stays (2–3 weeks) allow higher throughput, reaching 50–70 participants faster and generating more diverse phenotypes, but reduce per-participant event yield because parasomnia frequency is variable and some admissions will capture zero events—the protocol currently caps unproductive admissions at 20% before triggering criteria review, forcing a choice between strict preadmission screening (higher cost, slower recruitment) or accepting failed admissions and extending stays reactively (budget overrun). Balancing speed and capture quality determines whether the €3.8M budget achieves the minimum event count for Aim 2 analysis or requires external funding augmentation.
options: Enforce strict preadmission screening using a prospective 4-week home actigraphy run and structured bed-partner interview to confirm ≥3 episodes per week, admitting only high-confidence cases and accepting slower recruitment (20–25 participants per year) with near-certainty of multi-episode capture.

Adopt a variable-stay adaptive model where all participants enter for a standard 4-week baseline, but those reaching zero events by week 3 trigger an automated extension protocol (up to 2 additional weeks, funded from the contingency reserve) with the goal of capturing at least one event per admission.

Implement a rolling cohort with staggered 2-week admissions, accepting 25–30% unproductive stays as inherent noise, and use those cases to build a control-group comparison dataset on what nocturnal behavior looks like in participants who *think* they have parasomnia events but never demonstrate them clinically.
levers.review: Shorter stays reduce cost per participant but amplify the risk of zero-event admissions that generate only baseline sensor data with no episode phenotyping value—none of the three options directly address how to repurpose failed admissions or whether 20% unproductivity is operationally sustainable.

levers.name: Technician Annotation Authority and Real-Time Scoring Rigor
levers.consequences: Empowering night technicians to flag probable parasomnia events in real time (allowing triage escalation and event-driven PSG capture) accelerates clinical responsiveness and preserves sleep-state context, but introduces rater-dependent inconsistency—a tired or undertrained technician may miss subtle confusional arousals or misclassify sleep-stage-specific events, polluting the event-triage training dataset and inflating false-positive rates. The protocol mandates dual independent scoring afterward, but that occurs 48+ hours post-event when polysomnography context is lost and disagreement becomes expensive to adjudicate. Real-time technician judgment is operationally indispensable but methodologically risky without clear competency criteria and quality assurance.
options: Designate technicians as primary event identifiers with explicit training in AASM parasomnia criteria and mandatory weekly inter-rater agreement audits against video review and retrospective PSG analysis, creating a structured quality-feedback loop and accepting that some technicians will never reach ≥80% sensitivity.

Implement a dual-reviewer night model where one technician monitors sensors and participant safety while a second (lower-cost position) reviews video feeds in parallel 30-second-delayed playback, allowing collaborative event flagging and real-time discussion before escalation, increasing labor cost but reducing technician-specific bias.

Restrict technician real-time flagging to behavioral observations only (movement, vocalizations, unusual arousal patterns) without AASM-criteria scoring, reserving all parasomnia classification for the dual independent raters working from synchronized physiological data 24–48 hours post-admission, sacrificing event-driven PSG escalation but eliminating technician classification error.
levers.review: Real-time technician annotation enables clinical response and algorithm training but depends entirely on hire quality and fatigue state—none of the options directly address how to sustain consistent accuracy over 24 months without expensive turnover or whether weekly audits are sufficient to catch systematic bias.

levers.name: Enhanced PSG Montage Deployment Frequency and Sensing Cost Escalation
levers.consequences: Current protocol schedules enhanced PSG (standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, leg EMG) only on three fixed nights per participant (first, mid-stay, final) plus technician-flagged escalation nights; this minimizes per-participant sensor cost and technician calibration overhead, but risks missing the detailed physiological phenotype of events that occur outside scheduled nights, especially if episodes cluster unpredictably. Full continuous PSG would eliminate this blind spot but increases equipment utilization, technician setup time, and per-night cost substantially—the budget constrains the number of available PSG nights within the €3.8M envelope, forcing a choice between broad shallow sampling (all 8 suites nightly with dry EEG only) or deep sampling on fewer nights (full PSG on 3 scheduled nights per participant).
options: Retain the three fixed-night-plus-escalation model but add a fourth scheduled night at day 10 (early mid-stay inflection point where sustained parasomnia frequency patterns emerge), increasing per-participant PSG cost by approximately 25% and accepting that some sporadic events still occur between monitored nights.

Shift to a full-montage PSG-every-night model for the first 2 weeks of each admission, then revert to dry-electrode-only monitoring if no events are captured, backweighting equipment cost to high-yield early weeks and reducing later-stage setup burden while betting that event-free trajectories stabilize by week 3.

Implement a three-tier escalation protocol: baseline dry-EEG nightly, automatic PSG upgrade triggered after the first participant-reported event or technician flag (not contingent on schedule), and full in-situ PSG reactivation within 2 hours if a second event is flagged within 48 hours, making deployment reactive rather than fixed and requiring on-call technician availability.
levers.review: Fixed scheduling guarantees comparability but misses sporadic event phenotypes; fully reactive PSG maximizes capture but requires unsustainable technician availability and equipment turnaround—the three options do not resolve the cost-per-event trade-off or establish how to detect a true event clustering pattern versus random chance.

levers.name: Control Group Recruitment Scope and Baseline Contamination Risk
levers.consequences: The current plan includes matched controls under identical residential monitoring to benchmark event-triage tool false-positive rates against normal nocturnal behavior; this is methodologically essential for tool validation but requires recruiting and housing healthy adults (not parasomnia patients) for 2–8 week residential stays, a recruiting and safety challenge orthogonal to the patient pathway. Expanding the control cohort to 20–30 participants provides robust statistical power for false-positive thresholding but doubles staff coordination and facility occupancy complexity; conversely, minimal controls (n=5–10) compress costs but leave the false-positive rate estimate statistically underpowered, potentially biasing downstream algorithm specificity claims.
options: Recruit a small fixed control cohort (n=8–10) from sleep clinic volunteers, conduct their monitoring synchronously with patient admissions to share technician time, and accept statistical power limitations, focusing false-positive analysis on the aggregate absence of events rather than on individual-level noise characterization.

Establish a dedicated rolling control-recruitment pathway parallel to patient enrollment, aiming for 1 control participant per 3 patient participants over the 3-year window (approximately 20–25 controls), with separate scheduling to avoid overnight cross-contamination and allowing extended sensor-baseline analysis across seasons and circadian phases.

Use existing University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic healthy volunteers (staff, students, and registered research volunteers) rather than new external recruitment, compensating them at a lower per-night rate (€40 versus €80) and conducting all control monitoring in a single dedicated suite with fixed scheduling (e.g., weekly cohorts), trading recruitment flexibility for operational simplicity and data homogeneity.
levers.review: Robust controls are methodologically necessary but competing for facility resources and technician time with the primary parasomnia cohort—none of the options clarify how control-group monitoring interleaves with patient care or whether a 1:3 ratio is actually achievable without facility expansion.

levers.name: Dual-Rater Independence and Manual Scoring Throughput Sustainability
levers.consequences: The protocol mandates two independent AASM-trained raters score all nights and all flagged events post-hoc, ensuring rigorous event adjudication and enabling inter-rater reliability reporting; this is essential for credibility but creates a labor bottleneck—if a single trained rater can score approximately 4–5 participant-nights per week (assuming 8 hours per night of polysomnography data), then 50–70 participants with 2–8 weeks each generate a scoring backlog of 500+ nights, requiring ~2.5 FTE rater-years over three years. The €3.8M budget allocates personnel funds for the team but independent dual scoring is often outsourced or requires hiring additional scorers, compressing available funds for other functions or extending publication timelines.
